To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the bulbar ensemble burst amplitude decreased during the CS+, while the cortical ensemble burst amplitude increased during the CS+.
olfactory bulb and cortical high-frequency bursts are differentially modulated by conditioned olfactory stimuli, and that these modulations are learning related.

The amplitude of olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex EEG burst activity changes in response to conditioned stimuli, and these changes are spatially heterogeneous in both structures, with the greatest changes occurring in the region that is most phase lagged with respect to the ensemble average burst.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of the olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex in the formation of conditioned odor responses in rabbits and with the possible functional significance of the observed changes in bulbar and cortical electrical activity.
the question of whether the olfactory cortex can function independently of the olfactory bulb during the course of classical conditioning to odor stimulation.
the neural basis of learning and memory in the olfactory system of the rabbit.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, although olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex are both involved in the conditioned response, the olfactory bulb is more important for the initial response to the conditioned stimulus, whereas the olfactory cortex is more important for sustaining the response.
the olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex have different response properties to the same CS+ stimuli and that these response properties are related to the learning process.
the olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex respond in opposite ways to the CS+ during the course of conditioning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the olfactory cortex responds to the CS+ by an increase in burst activity while the bulb undergoes a learning-related reduction in burst activity, and this reduction is not uniform throughout the bulb but is greatest for the region that has the greatest lag with respect to bulb ensemble average activity.
the bulbar ensemble burst amplitude is reduced by conditioning to a greater extent than the cortical ensemble burst amplitude.
bulbar oscillations are modulated by the learning process in such a way that bulbar regions that are most sensitive to the CS+ undergo a decline in amplitude.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the olfactory cortex and bulb are not simply relay stations for olfactory information but are also sites where information is processed and where learning occurs.
the olfactory bulb does not respond to the CS+ in the same manner as it does to the unconditioned stimulus (US) or to the CS+ at the beginning of the experiment.
the olfactory cortex can be activated independently of the olfactory bulb by conditioned stimuli.
